title: When should ministers avoid acting unlawfully?
gist: New 2026 UK government guidance on legal risk drops all mention of the rule of law and reframes government legal advice around the likelihood of being challenged and losing, implicitly encouraging ministers to proceed with unlawful acts where litigation is unlikely. The author argues the rule of law requires compliance even when no court will hear the case.

insights.claim: The UK government's 2026 guidance on assessing legal risk removes the 2024 version's opening statement that the government must comply with domestic and international law, and does not mention the rule of law at all.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Signals a more risk-tolerant executive posture; watch for policies in areas that are hard to litigate (immigration, international law).
insights.quote: The 2026 version not only removes this introduction, it also does not even mention the rule of law at all.

insights.claim: The new guidance shifts the focus of government legal advice from compliance with the law toward whether the government will face a legal challenge and whether that challenge would succeed, effectively asking whether it can get away with a breach.

insights.so_what: Higher probability of policies later struck down or reversed; regulatory/legal-certainty risk for sectors exposed to executive action.

insights.claim: Many government actions face no realistic prospect of court review because international law is not normally justiciable in domestic courts, the government may control the evidence, and changes to court procedure and legal aid can make challenges impossible.

insights.claim: Critics portray government lawyers as 'unhelpful' and 'obstructive' and frame 'rule of lawyers' rather than 'rule of law' as a cause of public-sector failure, but the author argues blaming lawyers for their clients' faults is one of the oldest tricks, because lawyers advise and ministers decide.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Anti-lawyer rhetoric is a leading indicator of a government willing to push legal boundaries.

insights.claim: The UK government has ample legal resources — departmental lawyers, the Treasury Solicitor's department, the attorney general's office, plus external firms and barristers — so poor decisions are not due to lack of advice.

insights.claim: When the law is against the state, the state is usually well positioned to change the law or restructure its actions to minimise legal risk, so ministers who want 'robust' decisions must own them rather than breach the law quietly.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Legitimate route for policy change is legislation; watch for statutory changes rather than quiet non-compliance.

insights.claim: The author holds that the rule of law requires a lawful basis for every action and inaction of the state, and that government should comply with the law even where no court is likely to hear a challenge.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Frames the normative benchmark against which future UK executive conduct will be judged.
insights.quote: A falling tree in a forest should, at least in public law, still make a sound even if there is no court to hear it.
